newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Aussie dlr holds nerve as data fan rate fears.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Aussie dlr holds nerve as data fan rate fears.

text.p: The Australian dollar eked out some gains Tuesday even though shockingly weak sales data reminded one and all of the risk of a rate cut from today's RBA meeting.

Speculation of an easing has waxed and waned in the last few weeks but whether the bank will move come Wednesday morning remains anyone's guess. The drop in retail sales certainly added to the case for an immediate cut, but then the market had already sold the dollar down from 80 cents on just that belief.
That left dealers wondering if the market was so short a rally was possible whether the Reserve Bank moved or not and encouraged a bout of position squaring ahead of the big event.

By 4.55 pm (0555 GMT) the dollar was holding at US$0.7650/55 from US$0.7660 just before the data hit dealing screens. This was short of its offshore high of US$0.7695 but up on Monday's late US$0.7638/43 and last week's 11-month low of US$0.7595.
It was further underpinned by fresh weakness in the yen which saw it climb to 93.50/60 yen from 92.73/83 and to 58.4 in trade weighted terms from a previous 58.2 close.

The offshore bounce, the first serious rally in weeks, was largely inspired by a wire report that Finance Minister John Fahey expected the RBA board to wait for a ruling on a national minimum wage claim before deciding on policy.
But Fahey's office furiously backtracked today saying the minister only listed the economic considerations the bank was likely to look at when making its decision on rates.
"It was in no means a suggestion that they (the board) should wait, or could wait, or might wait," a spokesman said.

The market took the hint and the March 90-day bank bill future reversed an early 0.3 point drop to stand a basis point up at 94.37. That implied a rate of 5.63 percent compared to the present official cash rate of 6.0 percent.
Going by the sales data alone, analysts said it was hard to argue the market was wrong in its easier outlook.

Retail sales sank 1.0 percent in December compared to median forecasts of a 0.5 percent rise and a range of -1.0 to +1.5 percent. The trend series fell for the fifth month in a row, the poorest performance in the 35 year history of the data.
To underline the parlous state of the consumer real sales for the December quarter dived 1.3 percent, the largest drop in over 13 years, implying a 0.3 point detraction from GDP growth.

Hans Kunnen, chief economist at Colonial State Bank, said the data had prompted a downward revision to his forecast for Q4 GDP to flat from a 0.5 point rise. "We do not rule out the possibility that growth contracted," he added.
"While there are no guarantees that a further rate cut will stimulate jobs and spending, there are minimal risks in the current environment to cutting again," concluded Kunnen.
Some analysts thought the bank might still prefer to wait and see what effect, if any, its last two cuts in November and December had. There was also the question of wages to consider.
Key data on average weekly ordinary time earnings are due Thursday and should show a continued gradual slowing in annual wages growth to 3.6 percent from 3.8 percent.
That would be below the RBA's 4.5-5.0 percent danger zone, but somewhat historic since they cover the November quarter.
Instead, the RBA's eyes are mainly focused on a union claim for a national minimum wage hike worth around 8.75 percent which it has warned would threaten the low inflation outlook.
The claim is under review by the Industrial Relations Commission and, since no ruling is expected until the end of February or early March, the bank may decide a delay is prudent.

If the board does chose to move the most likely window will be the bank's regular morning operation at 9.30 am (2230 GMT) Wednesday morning. Silence would imply no change for the moment and propel the dollar to 77 cents, while a cut could see US$0.7595 re-tested. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
